name: Lies, Lies, Lies

items.name: KitKat for exams
items.fact: In Japan, “KitKat” sounds like “kitto katsu”, which means “you will surely win”. So people give KitKats to students as good-luck gifts before their exams.

items.name: Coca-Cola's Chinese name
items.fact: Before Coca-Cola chose an official Chinese name, some shopkeepers in China wrote it with characters that could be read as “bite the wax tadpole”. The official name means roughly “tasty and fun”.

items.name: Hungry Jack's
items.fact: In Australia, Burger King restaurants are called Hungry Jack's, because when Burger King arrived there, the name “Burger King” already belonged to a local takeaway.

items.name: Donald McDonald
items.fact: In Japan, the McDonald's clown is called Donald McDonald instead of Ronald, because “Ronald” is hard to say in Japanese.

items.name: Mr Clean's many names
items.fact: The bald cleaning-product mascot Mr Clean is called Meister Proper in Germany, Monsieur Propre in France and Mastro Lindo in Italy.

items.name: The Sorcerer's Stone
items.fact: The first Harry Potter book is called Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone in Britain, but the American publisher changed it to the Sorcerer's Stone, worried that children wouldn't pick up a book with “philosopher” in the title.

items.name: Inside Out's vegetable
items.fact: In Pixar's Inside Out, the little girl hates broccoli. In the Japanese version, it was changed to green peppers, a vegetable many Japanese children dislike.

items.name: Zootopia's news anchors
items.fact: In the animated film Zootopia, the news anchor is a moose in the US version, a panda in the Chinese version and a koala in the Australian version.

items.name: Pokémon's jelly doughnuts
items.fact: In the English version of the Pokémon cartoon, Japanese rice balls were called “jelly doughnuts”, even though the pictures still showed rice balls.

items.name: Walkers and Sabritas
items.fact: Lay's crisps are sold under different names in some countries: in Britain they are called Walkers, and in Mexico they are called Sabritas, with a very similar logo.

fakes.name: The moose that became a deer
fakes.fact: When a Swedish children's book about a moose was published in Japan, the moose was redrawn as a deer, because Japanese children had never seen a moose.

fakes.name: The train with white smoke
fakes.fact: In the Italian version of a German cartoon about a little steam train, its smoke was changed from black to white, because black smoke means a new pope hasn't been chosen yet.

fakes.name: Kimchi to cucumbers
fakes.fact: In the Polish version of a Korean cartoon, the characters' kimchi was changed to pickled cucumbers, so that Polish children would recognise the food.

fakes.name: A dog for every country
fakes.fact: The dog in a British cartoon series is a different breed in each country: a poodle in France, a dachshund in Germany and a chihuahua in Mexico.

fakes.name: Coffee into chai
fakes.fact: When an American superhero film was released in India, the hero's cup of coffee was digitally changed into a glass of chai in every scene.

fakes.name: The friendly horn
fakes.fact: A Japanese car company gives cars sold in Italy a softer, more musical horn, because Italian drivers use the horn so often that the normal one annoyed people.

fakes.name: The tea-glass card
fakes.fact: In the Turkish version of a Spanish card game, the cups on the cards were redrawn as small Turkish tea glasses.

fakes.name: Hockey on sand
fakes.fact: A Canadian ice-hockey video game was sold in Brazil with a “beach” version, where the ice was replaced with sand and the players wore shorts.

fakes.name: The renamed hedgehog
fakes.fact: The hero of a French children's book, a hedgehog called Piko, was renamed for Finland, because his name sounded like a Finnish word for “grumpy”.

fakes.name: The sausage dinosaur
fakes.fact: When an American dinosaur cartoon was shown in Germany, the main dinosaur was renamed because its name sounded like a German word for sausage.

fake: Give the story a short title: “the … that became a …”.
A name, a picture, a food, a colour, a sound.
The home country and the new country.
One or two steps: what it was before and after.
A language, a habit, a law or a belief in the new country.
A date, a number or a small problem it caused.
tips: Be specific: numbers, dates and real places make a lie believable.
Give it a small problem (“fans complained that it looked wrong”): perfect things sound fake.
Make both talks the same length and give them the same confidence.
Don't laugh. Decide now who says which one.
